utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor against Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Prosecution, appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager today, Ms. Janet Stewart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence teams, appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alex Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Tuesday, the 11th of January, 2005, I would like to bid welcome to everybody in the courtroom, to the accused, to the Defence teams, and to the Prosecution. Today we will proceed with the testimony of the witness that we heard yesterday. But before that there are a few issues to deal with. First of all, I'm going to ask the registrar to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now in open session we have to discuss the issue of the three documents which seem to have been forgotten yesterday when the list of documents was read out. The first document is dated 12th January, 1993, which originates from the 3rd Corps, and which was sent to the 17th Mountain Brigade and the 303rd Brigade. The second document is dated 12 January, again sent by the 3rd Corps to the 314th Motorised Brigade and the 7th Muslim Brigade -- 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and a document dated 13th of January, 1993, which originates from the 3rd Corps and which is marked by "urgent" and sent to all the brigades and municipal defence staffs. We have to give identification numbers to these documents. Does the Prosecution have any objections to these documents being admitted into evidence? Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Mr. Registrar, I'm going to give you the documents and can I please have the numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these documents will be admitted into evidence as follows: The first one, dated 12th January, 1993, as the ERN is 01822083, and it will be given a number, 1982 and the English translation will be DH1982/E. The second document bearing the date 12 January, 1993, and which does not have an ERN number but it does have an internal number, 102/33119 will be admitted into evidence as DH1283 and the English translation will be marked by E. And the last document is 01822089. This is the ERN number and it will be admitted into evidence as DH1984, and its translation will be 1984/E. And this concludes the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We had to deal with yet another problem. Yesterday I have already indicated that we are considering whether it would be useful to have a sitting on Wednesday, but finally we have decided that this sitting will be held tomorrow afternoon but it will not start at quarter past 2.00 but at 3.00. If this might be necessary and if we have to work longer, we will continue after 7.00 to make up for the lost time. So this would be it and now we would wish to see the witness being brought in into the courtroom. The Prosecution has sent us the list of documents that they might be showing the witness during their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all, let me check that you hear me. As I told you yesterday, today we are going to continue with your testimony. Today you are going to have to answer to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. After that, the Defence lawyers will re-examine you, and if necessary the Judges will also have questions for you. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Yesterday when we adjourned for the evening we were discussing the camp that you visited in early August 1993 with General Alagic, and I have a few questions about the persons you saw and briefly met with at this camp near Mehurici. Sir, to the best of your recollection, prior to that day had you ever seen any of those people that you met with before at any other location?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you hear me? These people that I met in the camp I had never seen before, either in Travnik or in any -- on any of the defence lines that I had inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time after that day when you met these people in Mehurici, did you ever see any of those foreigners or other people that you met at this camp on any other occasion at any other location?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that first meeting at the Mehurici camp, I saw these people on several occasions, but I could not place them. In other words, I couldn't say whether they belonged to a unit or not. I just saw them in the zone of combat responsibilities, given the tasks that I received from my superior, General Hadzihasanovic. At the end of the day, I didn't know Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond where they were. I knew that they were there, but I was not concerned with what they were doing and what units they were members of. In other words, I did see them in the area. I didn't see them that often, maybe one or two times, just passing by while I was tending to my tasks. So I was in no way directly connected to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you can remember, can you tell us where it was that you saw these people and what it was that you saw these people doing on this occasion or occasions after the meeting in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly saw them in Mehurici or in its vicinity. What they did, I don't know. Either I was passing by or they were passing by. I did not have any direct contacts with them. I didn't know what they were doing, what their task was, whether they had been given any task and who from. I was controlling the line that went from Mehurici towards Meokrnje and the Vlasic plateau. And I was passing by and inspecting that line, I would come across them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I understand what you say, sir, when you say you didn't know what they were doing or what their task was. But I guess my question is more along the lines of: What did you observe them doing? Were they simply standing on a street corner? Were they involved in what appeared to be military training? What exactly did you see these people doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be standing in the street or they would be passing in vehicles in one direction or another. If they had weapons, those would be rifles and they would be on their shoulders, which means that they were not ready for combat. There were individuals moving about, tending to their business. They didn't do anything specific when I saw them. I could not draw any conclusion as to what they were doing at that particular moment. I just saw them as I was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you said you may have seen them in vehicles. Can you tell us what kind of vehicles you remember seeing these persons in.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were either small-terrain vehicles, either Toyota or Pajero, small vehicles holding a driver, a co-driver, and two passengers in the back. And there were some parts where you could load some equipment on. So they were either Toyotas or Pajeros, those small, all-terrain vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of clothing did you see these people wearing, these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I already said that yesterday, but let me repeat. They wore camouflage uniforms, which was not complete and it did not look like the uniform that the BiH army troops wore. Those were incomplete camouflage uniforms, but they had shorts like trousers, they had wind jackets or jackets, and underneath the jacket or top part of the uniform, they wore some civilian clothes. And as I said yesterday, they also wore head scarfs or bandanas around their necks and their head pieces were not the types of hats that we were supposed to wear, that was part of the camouflage uniform. And they did not have any insignia, either on their shoulder or on the cap, while I have to tell you that we insisted in the BH army that all our troops wore insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did troops within the BH army begin wearing insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH army troops start wearing insignia on their sleeves and on their caps when the Territorial Defence was formed in May 1992. Then we wore the insignia of the BiH TO. And the official insignia were introduced at the beginning of 1993 when the regular army was established. In more specific terms, in Travnik, when the brigades were established, we received orders according to which we provided our troops with the insignia to be worn on the arms and on the caps. So from the end of 1992 and especially after the beginning of 1993, all the troops bore the characteristic insignia on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a couple of last questions about the meeting in the vicinity of Mehurici at the beginning of August, 1993. On the occasion that you met with these -- this small group of these foreign fighters, these Mujahedin, did any of those individuals introduce themselves to you by name, and, if so, do you remember the names of any of these individuals that you met with?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not introduce to us -- introduce themselves to us by names, but they greeted us with the characteristic Muslim greeting, Salam Alaikam. We also shook hands, although it was not their custom to shake hands. They never told us their names, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, line -- on page 8, line 7 where it says that they wore the characteristic insignia it says from the end of 1992 and especially after the beginning of 1993, all the troops bore the characteristic. However, the witness said, "if we were able to obtain them," and that was then followed by the characteristic insignia on their uniforms. So part of the sentence that the witness uttered was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One part of the answer was not translated, and what the witness said has to be added to the answer. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on any occasion of this meeting at the beginning of August, 1993, did you personally become aware of the names of any of these foreign Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did learn some of the names, but not through personal contact, rather I learned them from what other people said because I moved about among the soldiers. So I heard about a certain Musa or Vahid or something like that, Wahiudin, but I don't think I met them personally or had personal contact with them. However, through what people were saying on the lines, I learned that there were these certain people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us what you learned about these people from the soldiers on the lines. Can you recall what anyone told you about Mr. Wahiudin?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very specific, but in general when I was moving among the soldiers at the lines they would say that they had seen or heard that Wahiudin was fighting, organising, preparing, recruiting. They didn't say anything specific, he did or that specific things. But rather, it was the general sort of things that were said on the lines. The soldiers themselves avoided making any specific references, any direct references.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you know who Mr. Wahiudin was? Did there come a time when you learned anything about this person?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again that I heard in general that he was in the camp. I didn't know what his role or position was. I knew that he was one of the commanders or leaders. He was in some sort of hierarchy within that organisation, but I didn't know specifically what his position was, whether he had any rank, whether he had any military training or civilian education, I didn't know any of that. But I did know he was in there and that he did have some sort of post or duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you make reference to the camp or when you say "he was in there," are you referring to the Mujahedin camp near Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to, if we can call that a camp. I think we know what we are referring to. There was an organisation there with -- encompassing everything including accommodation and hygienic arrangements and so on. So it was really the place where they stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of General Alagic meeting with any of these Mujahedin on any occasions after this meeting you've told us about in early August 1993 near Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific because, let me repeat, the duties I was carrying out were not strictly -- did not strictly require that I escort General Alagic. The time I went with him as an operations man, he took me along so that I could see what the situation was together with him. But I had other tasks and duties. You have to understand that at that time we had two kinds of struggle going on, one against the Chetniks and the other kind of struggle which was not military, not with weapons, was concerned with logistics, the rear, and organising life and work in the depth of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond terrain. So I was absent from General Alagic's whereabouts very often, carrying out these other tasks. So I cannot be sure whether they met again or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, sir, other than this meeting in the beginning of August 1993 near Mehurici, you personally never met with them or attended a meeting with them at any other point in time or at any other place?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only time I had direct personal contact and some kind of conversation with them. Anything else, if it took place at all, was -- took place within another context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us yesterday that these Mujahedin were never under the command, your command, or under the command of any units of the Bosanska Krajina Operational Group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were not under the direct command of the operative group of the Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 615.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you if you've seen this document, P615, that's being shown to you. Have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read the document?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you then -- again with the assistance of the usher, if the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit P673. Sir, let me ask you first, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report by the commander of a subordinate unit, and I think I saw this document in the course of the regular reporting. We received many such reports from subordinate units describing the situation for a certain period or on a certain day, covering a longer or shorter period of time. So there were large numbers of such reports. It says here at 2300 hours the Mujahedin and so on and so forth, I think that this is an important element, there is some sort of slaughter mentioned here, so I think I would remember this. I did have most of these documents before me, so most probably I had this one, too, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, from the face of the document, can you tell me who this document was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to the operations centre of the Operative Group Bosanska Krajina, to the commander personally, so that the commander would be informed of the situation. It was addressed to the command of which I was a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on the 19th of August, 1993, what position within the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina did you hold?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander for operative and training matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us, because you've alluded to this, the fact that the document makes actually two references to the Mujahedin. There's the first one that you indicated, which is on page 2 of the English translation, but it makes reference to 2300, events in Guca Gora. And then if you look down three paragraphs after that first reference, there's another reference to the Mujahedin. Do you see that second reference, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the word "Mujahedin" is mentioned in only one place on this document, this is line 7 or 8, where it says: "The Mujahedins expelled three Croats from their houses in Guca Gora at 2300 hours, threatening them with slaughtering." So this is the only place where the word "Mujahedin" is stated or written down, if we're referring to the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me draw your attention to the bottom of the document above where there is a signature block. If you look at the far right-hand margin of the document on the third line from the bottom, the last word would seem to be Mujahedin. The copy is not maybe the best. Can you see what that paragraph says?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The rampage of the Mujahedins must be immediately stopped, particularly of the domestic ones, since if this is not done there is a threat that it might escalate and become an armed clash." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me ask you this as a professionally trained and career military officer: If the Mujahedin were not part of a subordinate unit of the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina, why would there be these types of references to the Mujahedin in an official report of a subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this written text, this report by the commander of a subordinate unit, every soldier and everyone who was not a soldier might conclude that they were not part of that unit because he never says in this text in the first platoon of the 1st Company, and so on and so forth, a Mujahedin unit did this or that. Rather, this can be interpreted to mean that there was a unit called the Mujahedin who were doing this and that in the area, and in my view he's asking for assistance from the operations group to solve this. Because he says that the rampage must be immediately stopped. So he's asking us for some sort of assistance to resolve this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why would that lower-level commander think that the operational group commander could solve this problem if the Mujahedin were not part of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it's very simple. A unit can be or not be in an area and it can be either subordinate or attached to a certain unit, or it can be engaged pursuant to orders of a higher command. And they might be carrying out tasks for this higher command, with the knowledge of the local commander, of course. So it doesn't follow that the commander of the area in which the unit is knows everything that the unit is doing. I am -- I'd like to say again that they were not under the direct command of the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group. I know that General Alagic used to say that they should be placed under the command of the OG, that they should be included in the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask now, sir, with again the assistance of the usher if the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit P665. Sir, let me ask you as a starting point, have you ever seen this document, P665, prior to today?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before, but when we formed this joint command there were many similar documents that came to us for our information. And whether I was physically present there in this joint command or not, I don't know. But this is the first time that I've seen this. I know that there were meetings and that I went out on the ground, but I'm certain that I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I show you this because in paragraph 3 there's reference to foreigners in the area of the 306th Brigade, and I'm wondering if you have any knowledge or information about the presence of foreigners in the area of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I think the witness said right away that he never saw this document before. We have had occasion to here officers of the 306th Brigade here, and from what the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic has told us we can see that even the commander of the 306th Brigade will testify here. Our objection is that this witness cannot interpret this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not asking the witness to interpret the document. I'm asking the witness if he's aware of any instances in which the commanders of the 306th Brigade lodged complaints up the chain of command concerning the presence of foreigners in the area of responsibility of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear the question? The Prosecution would like to know whether you heard from the soldiers that you visited on the front lines any objections, any questioning with regard to the presence of foreigners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can speak of -- with reference to your question, Your Honour, I know that in August of 1993 I Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond heard a lot of complaints from the soldiers in this unit. But this was three or four months after what is mentioned in this document. As I said, this is the first time I've seen this document. Maybe at that point in time I was not in the headquarters of the operations group, but I know that there were various reports. What I can say is that whenever we had contacts and conversations with members of the HVO, they always referred to soldiers who were members of the BH army as Mujahedin. They called the TO staff in Travnik the Mujahedin staff, even though our personnel was of mixed ethnic origin. There were Croats and Serbs and there was even a Jew as well as Muslims in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn for a moment, sir, to a slightly different topic. Can you give us the dates or the approximate dates that you served as the operations officer for the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I partly answered your question yesterday. According to the orders and the documents, this was in May. However, I was still the commander of the municipal staff when I was appointed to the joint command so that the time mentioned in the documents does not correspond to what I was actually doing at the time, from April until the time I was appointed to another duty, and that was in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So again, for the record, when you say "April or May," that would be 1993. The period from April or May 1993 through March 1994, you were the operations officer for the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina, the assistant commander for operations and training, I believe?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for operations and training, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the time period you were the assistant commander for operations and training within the OG Bosanska Krajina, can you tell us which units were part of the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group was formed as a temporary command in order to relieve the pressure on the communications in the direct command of the 3rd Corps, although there was some changes there. It was the 312th; the 306th; the 17th Krajina Brigade; the 27th Motorised Brigade, which was in the process of being formed; and then the 37th Mountain Brigade, after it was formed, entered into this group; then 308th OG West was then moved to the Bosanska Krajina OG; and the 325th Brigade in the Vitez area. Those were the brigades. I don't know if I've listed them all, but I think that's it. I'm now trying to remember whether I missed anything. That's it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us as a rough approximation of the geographic area that the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanska Krajina was responsible for the territories of the municipalities of Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Vitez, part of the territory on the Vlasic plateau, whether it belonged to the Kotor Varos municipality or not, I'm not sure, Travnik -- primarily Travnik, a part of the territory of Novi Travnik, and a part of the territory of Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told -- you mentioned the 27th Motorised Brigade. I'm wondering if you can recall when that brigade was formed, perhaps who its first commander was, and what was the area of responsibility of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically the forming of the brigade I think I said yesterday took place over a relatively long period of time. In any case, the order I think was in May but it was actually formed in early June. That's when part of the unit was lined up and that was the 27th Brigade. The first commander was -- oh, I know him. He's from Slovenia, but his name escapes me now although I do know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let me ask you if you can remember the area that the 27th Brigade was located in or was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when it was established, the 27th Brigade was established in the Travnik barracks. And when its units were established, when troops were recruited, their zone or -- in other words, its headquarters was in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me return and ask you a few questions about your role as the assistant commander for operations and training within the OG Bosanska Krajina. You told us a little bit about what your main responsibilities were, but would it be fair to summarise part of your responsibilities or an important part of your role one being whereby you were receiving and reviewing reports from subordinate units on a wide variety of issues concerning operational matters?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst other tasks, this was also my task. All the reports that arrived from units involved in combat reached me. I would sort them out, I would propose to the commander what could be done. A lot of these documents, since we didn't have our communications centre at the beginning, reached us through the communications centre of the 17th Krajina Brigade that had a communications centre. The person who worked in the centre would deliver these documents directly to General Alagic. In other words, some of the documents reached me personally and some of them reached the commander directly. However, since I cooperated with the commander, I was well abreast of the situation at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where was your office when you were the assistant commander for operations and training within the OG Bosanska Krajina? Where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially I did not have an office on my own. I shared the office with two or three persons. It was an office in -- attached to the Travnik barracks in a separate little building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, you've told us about receiving communications and reports from subordinate units of the OG Bosanska Krajina. Do you recall on -- ever receiving information where subordinate units lodged complaints concerning Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of those complaints, but those were communicated to the commander. There were very few written documents to that effect, or at least there were very few that reached me. In any case, this was more of an organisational problem that the commander of the OG had to deal with in talking to his subordinate commanders. If anybody asked me, it was my place to say I have that many people, that much equipment which could be used. All I could do was propose to the commander how these could be used. The final decision with regard to the organisation of any possible actions depended on the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, any specific instances where the commander of the OG Bosanska Krajina received complaints concern the Mujahedin? When I say "complaints," I mean complaints from subordinate units of the operation group. Can you recall any of the specific complaints, what those complaints were about?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for operations and training; however, I spent very little time with the commander. When he inspected his units, he would take somebody from the other bodies that could be of use to him, for example, the person who was in charge of morale and security. So I can't say that I was present when anybody complained and said in very concrete terms, General, we have this or that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So what you're telling us then, sir, was that you were aware that there were complaints from subordinate units concerning the Mujahedin, but you are not aware of the substance of those complaints?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a play on words. I was aware of the substance; however, I can't provide you with the concrete detail of when those complaints were lodged. Like I said yesterday, the Mujahedin recruited soldiers from the existing units and some young men were attracted by good uniforms, by weapons, by food they gave to their families, and they left their units. And these were the biggest objections and complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us yesterday that - and this was on page 59 of the transcript yesterday - you said: "As far as I know, the Mujahedin or the El Mujahed detachment were never placed under the command of the Bosanska Krajina OG, at least not on the basis of the documents available, nor did they ever become part of the structure of the Bosanska Krajina Operation Group." Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Do you remember testifying about that yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the orders from the commander of the 3rd Corps concerning the resubordination of the El Mujahed detachment with respect to the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this order; I didn't see it, however. At this point I would like to provide you with some explanation as to what is the meaning of subordination, resubordination, detachment, because all these elements imply different elements of responsibility. If some unit is resubordinated, then it has to be accounted for when it comes to food, artillery support. So we had to make a difference between subordination, resubordination, attachment for the completion of a task. If somebody is attached for the completion of a certain task, then this unit is not part of the strength because some units did join the OG but they were not on the strength of the OG. If I had said this, which I did and I adhere by that, they were never organisationally part of the OG. This order, I can't say whether I saw it or not, but I know that the command of the 3rd Corps ordered for this unit to be either resubordinated or attached to the OG for the completion of a certain task, and I adhere by that. But I can also state here that this doesn't mean that they were an organisational part of the OG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask, again with the assistance of the usher if the witness can be shown two documents, Prosecution Exhibit 792 and Prosecution Exhibit 440.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something that my learned friend is aware of. The time given to the Defence during their examination-in-chief has now been overstepped by the Prosecution. We would now like to know, because of the planning of our following witnesses, how much longer will the Prosecution need. This will serve our planning process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has not noticed that, but I believe that this will be useful. Mr. Mundis, you have taken longer than you were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, based on the calculations that we've kept here, and I understand it's the official registry times that are important, but by the estimates that we've kept I still have approximately ten minutes before I would even hit the point of using the same amount of time as my learned colleagues. At any rate, I would expect to be finished within approximately ten minutes. But I -- if in fact the registry informs me that I have exceeded my time, then we will adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar tells us that you have another ten minutes. So the Defence has to re-calculate the time. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've been shown two documents, Prosecution Exhibit P792 and Prosecution Exhibit P440. Let me ask you, sir, if you recall having seen those documents prior to today.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document dated 28 August 1993 and the number that you've mentioned which I can't see, I have never seen before. This is an order which was sent directly to the 306th. And even if the Bosanska Krajina OG had been notified of it, I didn't see it. The order sent on the 6th of September, 1993, seven or eight days later, again I see in this document that it has never been acted upon, it hasn't been followed through. Again, it is ordered that the independent unit, El Mujahed, should be resubordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG for combat according to the plan of the BK Operations Group. I can explain that if you want. At this moment this unit was not part of the structure and the organisational strength of the OG. It didn't want to, it could not be resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. The second order followed that and in this order it says that this unit should be resubordinated to the OG. And I did see this second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, again as a professionally trained and career military man, what would you have to say about the fact that the commander of the 3rd Corps was ordering this El Mujahed unit to be resubordinated? You're telling us that unit was not part of the OG Bosanska Krajina, but certainly Commander Hadzihasanovic was ordering this unit to be resubordinated to the OG Bosanska Krajina. Do you have any explanation or can you shed any light on that based on your professional experience?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really very simple. The order pursuant to which this unit is resubordinated to the unit that is part of the strength of the Bosanska Krajina OG is a mistake because this could not be ordered. Our subordinate unit could not receive direct units from our superior command, and since this order was never followed through it was ordered that they should be resubordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG and that the commander of the BK OG should use the unit as he saw fit. This doesn't mean that they were on the strength or in the organisation of the OG. I have to say that the corps commander did have the commanding right to deploy a unit directly because the order given to me by telephone or in writing is the same to me when it comes to subordination and hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But again, correct me if I'm wrong, sir, I believe yesterday, again page 59, lines 6 through 8 of the transcript, you testified that the El Mujahed unit or part of that unit participated with one of your brigades in some combat operations, and that resulted in an unusually high number of casualties. Did I understand your testimony about that correctly?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, and I believe that this was in mid-September. It was sometime around the 17th or the 18th of September. And the unit in question is the 17th Krajina Brigade. They were not either subordinated or resubordinated, they were attached to execute a task in the sector belonging to the 17th Krajina Brigade. Within that sector they had their own task, which they either completed or not completed maybe because of their own mistake, maybe there was no coordination, or maybe there was no cooperation, and that is why the 17th Krajina Brigade suffered enormous loss within a very short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the only occasion that you have knowledge of or recollection of in which the El Mujahed unit was attached to or operated in conjunction with units of the OG Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only situation that I'm aware of, the only situation where they worked together in the zone of responsibility of the Bosanska Krajina OG. And this was within the combat area where the HVO fought in Vitez against the BH army. At that time I was in a different part of the zone of responsibility where the event that you mentioned a while ago took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. You have exhausted your time, and now I'm turning to the Defence for their re-examination. I am going to give you the floor after the break. We have some five or six minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kulenovic, I have a few questions for you. Yesterday when you were answering my learned friend's questions you said that the first rumours about some foreigner fighters from the Arabic countries reached you sometime in the summer of 1992 when you were in the Visoko theatre of war. My question to you is: At that time did you check in one way or another if the rumours were true? Did you want to learn the truth behind those rumours?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what you have just mentioned and I repeat that the first rumours involving the Mujahedin reached me sometime in July or August while I was staying in the Visoko front line. I didn't check that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond information. I didn't want to find out whether there is any truth in that information. I was preoccupied with something else. We did not have the army, the army had not been established. We had a group or a mass of poorly armed men that had to be put in some order. This was my main preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also stated that you saw some foreigners from African and Asian countries in Travnik in the year 1992, and they mostly appeared as humanitarian workers. You also told us that the War Presidency had logistic tasks to support the army. As the commander of the Territorial Defence staff, did you ever directly talk to those humanitarian workers from African and Asian countries, or whether in Travnik that communication was with the civilian bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the initial period I never personally spoke to those humanitarians because we had a gentlemen's agreement to deal with all the issues with the commander of the logistic centre of the Defence staff of Travnik. This is just the working term that we used. So whatever problems we had, I spoke to this person that was appointed by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This logistics centre of the municipality you've just told us that it was established by the Municipal Assembly. This logistics centre, was it under the authority of the civilian bodies of authority or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This logistics centre was under the authority of the civilian bodies, and we had a gentlemen's agreement which bore on friendly to deal with problems. In other words, I had a right and an obligation to submit my list of requirements, and they would act on those requirements and would deliver whatever was necessary to the military structures and the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the first time you saw armed Mujahedin was when you were with Commander Alagic and when you entered their camp or the place where they stayed not far from Mehuric. Was that your first encounter with persons from African and Asian nations which acted as soldiers at the same time because they were armed?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my first direct physical contact with these people from African and Asian countries who wore arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The question -- the Prosecutor has just shown you a document that originated from the command of the 3rd Corps, pursuant to which the El Mujahed unit was subordinated to the Bosanska Krajina OG for the execution of a task. You've just seen this document. And also, you have told us that you know that they did participate in some combat operations in mid-September, together with the 17th Krajina Brigade. Tell me please, your information about the existence of this order, did it indicate to you and were you aware of that time that Commander Alagic and the commander of the 3rd Corps tried to place that unit under control and command and also the experience of the 17th Krajina Brigade speaks to the contrary. In other words, they could not be placed under any control. Would that be your experience from the time that you spent in the OG?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's a compound question. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's a compound and leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is indeed complicated; it is compound. Can you please break it down into smaller pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, from your contacts with Commander Alagic after your attempt to enter the camp, could you conclude -- did you have information that there were efforts in place to place these people under control, or would the opposite be true? I don't know how else to put that question.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. A little while ago in answering the Prosecutor's question I said that we tried to place these people under control and insert them among our ranks. After my first meeting with them at the facility that you refer to as camp, and after the end of that visit and the attempt to reach some sort of agreement, General Alagic used some very harsh words, I can't quote him, but he said more or less, These men should either be disarmed or chased away to where they came from. This is just a rough quote or a summary of General Alagic's opinion. I believe that he spoke on several occasions to his superior command. He wanted this unit to be, as he said, soldierised and placed under control. He wanted them to be drilled and trained. In any case, an attempt was made to place that unit under control and to put them in the function of the armed combat under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, given the experience that you have and about which you spoken to this Trial Chamber, when you were attached to the OG, when you were attached to the 17th Krajina Brigade, can you tell us could they effectively be placed under the control of the Bosnian army despite your efforts?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this combat operation I was in a different place, on a different location. However, based on all my previous knowledge and based on the subsequent conversation with the participants in that action, this unit was not an organic part of the 17th Brigade. They just performed tasks. They were given their axis, their task, and as far as I know, as far as I'm familiar with the military matters, they were never part of the 17th Brigade. They were never either subordinated or resubordinated. They wanted to be independent, they wanted to perform their task independently at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the previous answer to my learned friend you said that you know that they participated together with the 17th. But now if I understand you well, you're saying -- you are talking about things in plural. What can you tell me about your personal knowledge of the participation of the El Mujahed unit together with another unit from the OG? In other words, according to your personal knowledge in 1993, how many times the El Mujahed detachment participated in combat together with some other unit of the OG? Was it just that one occasion when they were attached to the 17th or were there any other cases?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of just one specific case into which we had an insight, where we could exert some sort of partial control and command; this was in the second half of September when they sort of cooperated with the 17th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You entered with Commander Alagic their camp in the vicinity of Mehurici. Did you know whether there existed some other places in the territory where the units of the Bosanska Krajina OG were active, where there were also Mujahedin? Did you know of any other such places or was this the only place that you visited and that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the only place that I was aware of that they had their base and that they stayed there. If there had been any other places, I was not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question with regard to the questions put to you by my learned friend is again connected with the logistical centre of the War Presidency. Tell me please, who did the logistical centre provide assistance to? Who did the civilian authorities provide aid to from this logistical centre?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this logistical centre, which had been established by the municipality and was under their authority, under the authority of the civilian authorities, most of the aid that arrived, I don't know where from and how, was spent on refugees or people who had been expelled from the territories that I have already mentioned. So whenever there were different waves of refugees and expelled persons, several tonnes of food were used for them, as well as clothes, food, blankets, and everything else that was necessary for their accommodation. A lot of that aid was used for the purposes of the TO staff. Once the units were formed, this served to provide logistical support for these units. Also the beneficiaries of that aid were other civilian structures. For example, I received a tonne of washing powder and I provided the hospital with 700 kilos of washing powder, for which I was praised by the doctors, by the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond patients, because the situation in the hospital was critical at times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that this would be the last question. However, the document that my learned friend showed you as originated from the 306th Brigade in which the Mujahedins are mentioned in two places, the question was put to you whether it would be normal for a unit to send a report to the superior command and mention somebody who is not on its strength. My question to you: As a soldier, tell me, would it be normal for one unit to uniform its superior command of every fact that might have any sort of influence on the morale and the combat readiness of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be very direct in my answer. Not only is it normal, it is an obligation of every unit. If a unit enters the location of another unit, that latter unit has to inform its superior command and ask for explanation as to why that happened. So not only is it normal, but it is also the obligation of the unit to report on any other unit being deployed in its area of responsibility asking for further explanations from its superior command. As a lower-ranking commander, I don't have to know what my superior commander is thinking or doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also as a professional soldier, can you tell me, would it be normal or is it normal that a unit informs its superior command about those who have nothing whatsoever to do with the army requesting from the superior command to address the issue or forward it to a higher place that can address the issue. Would it be normal or would it be an exception?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this is not an exception, this is normal, because any such thing as a direct bearing on the system of command and control of the unit where this unit is deployed. So it is normal and it is a must for such a unit to inform its superior command and even send it its proposal for the solution to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Given your overall experience in the year 1993, would you be able to say if there was any other -- any level in the BiH army would be the level that could deal with the issue of Mujahedin and their presence in the area. Was that an issue that had to be resolved by the army or could be resolved by the army?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question and I can only tell you one thing. To the extent that I stayed in the territory covered by various units, in my view this unit was never part of any of the units that we have mentioned so far. And my opinion at the time was that this unit could not be controlled or commanded. I can't tell you anything about our higher-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to make a technical break. It is 10 to 4.00. We should resume at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. I am going to give the floor to the other Defence team for their re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have a few questions to put to you. The Judges search for the truth and have the right to put the questions to the witness arising from the questions put to the witness from -- by the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few issues to clarify with you, sir. You told us that when you were educated by the JNA to become a JNA officer you specialised in reconnaissance and sabotage. Is that what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that during your activities within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina you also worked in the area of sabotage and reconnaissance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could have done such work because the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina might have been more successful. However, as the army as an armed force had not been formed. In view of our equipment and materiel and other logistical support, it was not possible either to prepare such a unit or carry out such activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You left the BiH army when, in what year?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the BH army, is that what you asked me? I didn't leave the BH army; I remained within the BH army structure and my last job was in the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of BH in the agency for monitoring and controlling weapons. And now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your last job in the army then would have to correspond to a certain rank. What was your last rank?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My last rank was that of colonel. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what I wanted to hear from you because when you are responding to questions it seemed to me that you were a high-ranking officer, and the fact that you left the army as colonel confirms this. You explained to us that you carried out inspection of the front lines. The Defence showed you a document showing that you were a member of the joint command. Can we conclude from this that in the operations group, that is the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group and in your various activities, you had a certain level of responsibility which was of medium importance or great importance. What could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to explain something. There was a difference that the HVO insisted upon. There was the joint command and the common command. I was a member of the common command, not the joint command. Joint would mean that they were one and the same; and the common means that they carried out certain tasks together. When I was carrying out my duties in the common command, my tasks and duties were of a medium level of responsibility. Roughly speaking, I gathered and processed information and I presented all this information together with my own opinions and suggestions to the higher-level command. And I toured the troops on the ground and I made proposals as to how certain problems should be solved, having to do both with the army and with the organisation of life in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your reply to the Judges shows that there were in fact two structures. There was a joint level and a common level. So these were two structures, and you say you were in the common command. When responding to the question on page 20, line 20, of the record, and this was in connection with the Mujahedin, you said the following, and I quote: "They carried out recruitment, or rather they tried to recruit people from already existing units." Do you confirm that you said this?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because indirectly they took these people away from the regular units by offering them food, clothing, other equipment, because they realised that as there was a general lack of resources these people would go where they could have something to gain. And this affected the situation in the units that these people left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, to the best of your knowledge, how many men left the regular units in order to join the ranks of the Mujahedin? Are you aware of any numbers? Do you know approximately how many men there were?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but I can give you a rough estimate. Many young men left because they received material means but they soon came back because their code of behaviour, the religious life to which the young men from Bosnia and Herzegovina were not used -- because they had a different way of expressing their faith and they were not used to the rigours of this religious life, so they came back. There was a lot of movement to and fro. They would stay there briefly and then come back, so I can't tell you exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so you do not have a number. When you learned that a soldier had left his unit and joined the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mujahedin - and I am addressing you now as a professional soldier - did the military hierarchy institute a procedure for desertion against such a young man who left his unit, to the best of your knowledge? I'm putting this question to you because we have seen documents of the 3rd Corps saying that deserters should be prosecuted. That's why I'm putting this question.

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear to me and I can respond very briefly or I can expand on my answer. The units did take certain measures. For the most part, the commanders or assistant commanders for morale, religious matters, and so on tried to talk to the parents or the close relatives of the soldier to try to get him to come back. In the meantime, there would have been a record made of this and certain measures taken. During my testimony I have already said that the brigade police could not penetrate into this camp. That has often been mentioned in order to interview a soldier and carry out their job, actually. I can add that usually it was the parents or the people, whether we wish to admit it or not, accepted the Mujahedin unit because they were providing support and help. And the parents would often say, Well, I want my son to fight for the freedom of our people. It didn't matter where, with what units. So this did cause certain problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but independently of the parents did the army itself take any measures? Did it sanction desertion? Because in any army in the world, deserters are punished. That's the question I'm putting to you. At your level of activity did you know that punishments had been meted out for soldiers who joined the Mujahedin and later returned because this was not what they had expected? Were there such punishments?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, there were punishments and certain measures were taken to punish such actions. The documents pursuant to which this was done is something I haven't seen. But I know we had a relatively small number of men, relatively little equipment and weapons, and all these young men who came back after certain measures, regardless of the severity of these measures, because of the needs for fighters were sent back to their units. For example, on the front lines I would punish any kind of violations such as drunkenness and so on and so forth. The men would be sent to do some necessary task. That's how these issues were resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now in connection with what you have just been telling us about. When you were with General Alagic in this camp near Mehurici, you said quite spontaneously that General Alagic told you that they were to be soldierised, transformed into soldiers. When you went to visit them, what was the aim of this visit? Was the purpose of the visit to tell them that they had to be integrated into the structure of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was this the main goal of your visit? Or was it simply establishing contact with them? Can you tell us more about this? Can you explain what the goal of the visit to these people was?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The simplest explanation would be to say that General Alagic, and I with him as his immediate subordinate, went to the camp for several reasons. The first of these were the frequent complaints of lower-ranking units against the presence of these people and the problems that have been mentioned and to integrate them into the structure. And the second reason was, if we managed to integrate them into the structure to see how they might possibly be used in combat, in specific combat activities. After we completed this visit, I said I can't recall the exact words, but what was said they had to be soldierised, transformed into soldiers. We went to see how many of them there were, to try and put them under some sort of control. Now, whether General Alagic had any orders from a higher command or any other information, I don't know. But in my view, that was the aim of the visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to see them you mentioned a number. You said that some were armed and others were not. On the day you went to that camp, how many of them where were approximately, more or less?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that yesterday that I saw four of Afro-Asian origin, and three of them had weapons; these were rifles slung on their backs. And I think there were seven or eight who were at some distance from us. So we only had contact with those three men in that little hut where we were sitting, and we tried to reach some sort of agreement with them. So three inside, four armed, and seven or eight a bit further off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for clarifying this. You said that General Alagic said: "They should be disarmed or sent back to where they came from." These words by General Alagic can also be seen in the documents. If we had time we would show you that, but unfortunately we don't have the time. Can you confirm, however, that General Alagic personally said that they had to be either disarmed or sent home? Is this what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like to clarify. General Alagic -- in Bosnia we only speak well of the dead, but he used some worse words, words that were not as nice which I would not like to repeat now. But the meaning was that they should be either disarmed or disciplined or sent away. That would be the main purpose of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I will put to you a question that I usually put to every witness. For me as a Judge this question always arises; I always ask myself this. Tell me, how is it possible that some 20 men at the most in that camp - you say there were four of Afro-Asian origin and there were eight or nine of them all together - how could it happen that 10 or 20 persons can represent such a force in comparison with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina about which a general testifying before the Tribunal said was that there were 32.000 people under the command of the 3rd Corps. So how is it possible for 20 people to stand up to 35 or 32.000? Can you explain this or should we seek for another explanation? The Defence put a similar question to you. In your view, did the solution have to come through the army or through some other institution? What can you as a soldier and high-ranking officer say in reply to this question that we are all asking ourselves?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try, although you have put a number of specific questions to me. I don't know whether there were 15 or 20 or more men; I don't know. But in the period we are talking about, on the one hand we have the Serb/Chetnik aggressors; on the other hand we have the HVO which at every point in time was doing its best to cause a conflict and to minimise the role and function of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was said to be an illegal force of the force of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it should be put under the control of the legitimate authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the HVO. I had a meeting with General Blaskic and General Kordic. When I went to see Blaskic to solve a problem, Kordic wanted to throw me out, saying that I was illegal. I think I mentioned that General Blaskic and I had worked together in the former JNA and he had learned a lot from me, speaking conditionally, and I solved a lot of things together with him. So we had the Chetniks, we had the HVO on the other side, we had poverty, hunger and, speaking in military terms, there were no conditions to prepare for combat activity. You say a small force. Well, yes, objectively it's a minimal force. In military terms it would not be taken into consideration as a force that could have a decisive impact. However, in view of the situation I have just described, we had to take care of every man, every man who could give us a drop of milk, every person who could give us a bullet or two. I personally led soldiers who I would give 15 bullets each before they were sent to carry out a task, whereas normally this would be -- the kit would be 150. In other words, I led people into war, sent them to their deaths, with 15 bullets in their hands. We needed all sorts of things, and that's why both I and General Alagic - and most probably the higher command, but I wouldn't like to comment on that - tried to get these people to become soldiers and to carry out the same role as the army as a whole. Because in my view, the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond army was very well-consolidated and ordered compared to the situation we had, the materiel situation, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have to draw a conclusion that you did not have the military means to face a group of that force because your men, your troops, were not well-equipped and you had difficulties with that. Is that the gist of your answer?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one part of the answers that I've provided. Yes, we didn't have enough materiel means and we had to save every single bullet to fight the real enemy. And this group, they could have been of some use to us if we have been able to organise them and place them under control. I'm speaking conditionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much. You have answered the Judges' questions and the two parties have the right to put questions to you arising from the Judges' questions, either to clarify the answers that you have provided or because they have some other reason to re-examine you. First I'm going to ask the Prosecution whether they have any questions to put to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now the Defence. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a few questions. The other Defence team does not have any questions, but I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kulenovic, the Presiding Judge has asked you about what you saw on that day and wanted to know the number of the Mujahedin who were there on that day. Did you know at all what was the number of persons who were accommodated, either in that camp or somewhere else where our units were active? Did you ever know the number of these men?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, and I am going to provide you with a clear answer. I never knew the exact number of these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kulenovic, were you aware of the number of the local men who joined them for various reasons or those who supported them for various reasons?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, how many joined them or supported them. I've just told the Presiding Judge that there were men who joined them and they returned to our ranks. How much and to what extent they supported them, I don't know. But I only know that they went just to take some provisions from them and return with those. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge asked you something that is very important and that reappears in this trial, and that is the question of why an armed force was not used against these people. And you have provided a partial answer. My additional question to you is as follows: As a professional soldier can you tell us, in order to carry out a military operation would it have been necessary for you to know the number, the place, the equipment, the level of education, and everything else that the people that you are about to fight against have at their disposal? Would that be important for you to know?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer professionally. The armies of the world use different methods in order to acquire data on the enemy. One of those means is to acquire intelligence during combat. We could have engaged in combat in order to locate a block, to destroy or capture these people and so on and so forth. However, let me say something else. There was a lot of smuggling going on through the Vlasic plateau where there -- this smuggling involved a lot of civilians and soldiers. The command of the OG Bosanska Krajina carried out a blockade together with the military police and the police forces of brigades that were on the ground and they managed to break that smuggling chain. The BiH army was in a position and was able to carry out such an operation, but they were wanted to know what the final result would be. We didn't know the exact number or location, but if we wanted -- if we had wanted to find out we could have done it forcibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were aware of the situation and the importance of saving your men and every bullet, would it have been necessary for you to make an estimate as to -- if such a combat -- such a fight had taken place, would that have caused a certain degree of fighting between you and the local population that supported the Mujahedin? Was that one of the elements that you had to take into account and assess?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me re-organise your question a little. You said whether this was important. I would say whether this was decisive. And I would say that this was this - a decisive element. If such a conflict had started, then the people who supported the BiH army and provided them with logistical support would have turned against the army and the BiH army would have certainly enjoyed much less support if such a conflict had started with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify what you have just said for the benefit of the Judges. Is that the reason why you said that this could not be resolved by the army but that it had to be resolved in some other place?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been resolved physically, by military means, but for the other reasons that I've just mentioned we avoided that, a physical showdown. Instead of using force, we resorted to some other means. We tried to involve politics in order to resolve that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to one of the questions put to you by the Presiding Judge you told us what General Alagic's comment was after your meeting in the camp. If I understood you well he said first that they had to be soldierised, turned into soldiers and used as such; and the second time he said they should be disarmed and chased away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was no first and second time. There was just the first part of his comment when he said that they had to be soldierised, turned into soldiers, and the second part which was, or alternatively they should be disarmed and chased away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have testified about the attempt of turning them into soldiers and using them in combat together with the 17th Brigade. Tell me, please, this attempt to use them as soldiers in your view as a soldier, did it prove that this was next to impossible? Let me not put words into your mouth. How would you -- what would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Men are always susceptible to influence; however, these people were not susceptible to influence because they didn't want to be turned into soldiers the way we, the army of BiH, wanted to have them. And their use, the way they wanted to be used, in this specific case was a failure when they were used together with our units that performed a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question arising from the Judge's question. When you were explaining why you couldn't enter a conflict with these groups, could you also tell the Trial Chamber what were the basic problems and tasks that the OG Bosanska Krajina faced in the summer of 1993. Was that the Defence from the Chetniks, the Serbian and the Chetnik aggressors, the fight with the HVO in the Lasva valley, the aim of which was to keep a certain part of that area, or to contain this group of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have already provided a good part of my answer in your question. At the beginning of my testimony I said that at the moment the defence staff of Travnik was formed, the most important thing was for us to defend ourselves and to prevent the further breakthrough of the Serbian and Chetnik aggressor in that. The second problem was to be as successful in fighting against the HVO as much as we could. At the beginning, the HVO was taught to cooperate with us in the fight for an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was proven to be wrong eventually. And the third problem was looking after the population and everybody else.
