And our last -- if you want a hierarchy, the last problem would be the internal fight for the organisation of certain units and placing them under very stringent control. This may be just my opinion. We looked after every man, after every bullet. On Vlasic plateau, one-third of our Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond OG was there defending the plateau from the Serbian and Chetnik aggressor, at least one-third if not one-half was on the lines fighting the HVO. So we had one-fourth less troops who were either resting or doing other thing which all this is against any military norm of using troops to perform any tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now finally my last question since you have provided a very good explanation. As a soldier, you know and I know as a lay person that every commander cares about the life of every soldier. Given into account all of these elements and your experience when only during one hour of fighting involving the Mujahedin, 12 members of a brigade were killed and over a hundred were wounded, was there any commander who could afford himself a luxury to start fighting a group that proved to be so dangerous when it came to casualties?

utterances.speaker: AHMED KULENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the word luxury; every commander could afford such a luxury; however, the final result would be a disaster. It would be an ultimate luxury to start such a fight in which so many casualties could be expected. No commander wanted to do that. They didn't dare do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, your testimony is now concluded by the answers that you have provided to various questions. We would like to thank you for your personal contribution to the search of truth. You have answered the questions put to you by both parties. I can only wish you a happy journey back home to your country, and I wish you the -- a good year on behalf of the Trial Chamber and a pleasant retirement. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Same to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we bring the next witness into the courtroom, I believe that Mr. Registrar has some corrections to make.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just two corrections with regard to the documents that have been admitted into evidence. In the first part of our session today, the first correction is relative to the document that was admitted as a document under seal as DH168; it is actually the Prosecution document which is P168. And the second document is the one that was admitted under DH1983. There has been an error here. The document is DH1983, and the translation is DH1983/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We are awaiting the arrival of the next witness. And in the meantime account Defence tell us how much time they have envisaged for the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have envisaged an hour and a half, but I'll make sure to curtail that by at least 15 minutes. The witness tomorrow will require less time and I believe that today and tomorrow we will be able to complete the testimony of both witnesses that have been envisaged for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to thank you for this information and your effort. And while we are waiting for the second witness to arrive, it will take some time because the first witness has to be taken out of the Tribunal and the second witness brought in. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. According to our records, there were a few documents, perhaps four documents, that were new documents that were shown to the last witness. I don't know if the Defence is planning on tendering those into evidence or if we're going to wait for a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe we could benefit from this time and regulate the admission of documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have shown several documents to the witness that have already been tendered through General Merdan, and we only wish to tender document 0591, 1169, 0774, and 1501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you wish to tender four new documents into evidence, 0591, 1169, 0774, and 15050 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake. The first document is not 0591 but 0951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This has to be corrected. It is 0951. Mr. Mundis, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, you have the floor. Can you give us the numbers for these documents. Mr. Usher, can you please go and fetch the next witness in the meantime. Everybody has a task here. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The four documents are as follows: DHD [as interpreted] 51 [Realtime transcript read in error "59"], with the translation, DH951/E; the next one, DH1169, and the English translation DH1169/E; and the next one is 774, and the translation 774/E; and finally the last document, the fourth document, DH1501, and the English translation 1501/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But I believe that we have a mistake in the transcript on line 12. It says here that the document is DH79 [as interpreted]. I believe that this is a mistake. This should be DH951. Can you please have a look at line 12 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. President. There has been a mistake in the transcript and the document number is -- the documents are 951, 1169, 774, and 1501. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, this is one fuzzy one. Again I've made a mistake. It's too late now. Luckily enough we've only had four documents on the agenda. I apologise, we have dealt with the documents. We wanted to make use of the time between the departure of the previous witness and your arrival. Before I go on, I would like you to confirm that you hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Defence witness. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would like to know who you are and that's why I would kindly ask you to give me your name, last name, the date of birth, the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vezir Jusufspahic, 23rd February, 1950, in Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have a profession? If you were a member of the military, what military was that and which units did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 I was working in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica, and later on I joined the ranks of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the BiH army, were you a member of a brigade or a command? What unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond before an international Tribunal or before a national court about the things that happened in your country in the years 1992 and 1993? Or is this the first time you testified about these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time to testify. I've never testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is handing out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence lawyers, I need to provide you with some explanation that will facilitate these proceedings. First you have to answer the questions that will be put to you by the Defence lawyers. You have already met with them. After that stage, the Prosecution sitting on your right will also be asking you questions, and their questions are called cross-examination. The Prosecution will be given the same time as the Defence. If the Defence is given one hour, the Prosecution will also be given one hour. After that stage, the Defence teams will have the right to re-examine you. After that, the three Judges sitting in front of you may also have some questions for you. Most of the time when the Judges do have the questions, it is to clarify things in order to find out the truth or to elaborate on the issues that you have tackled during your testimony. I need to inform you of two other things that are also important. You have just sworn to tell the truth, which means you are not to provide -- give us false testimony. This would be an infringement punishable by law. And the second thing that I have to inform you about is the fact that the witness has the right and the duties, the duty is to answer questions, and the right of the witness is not to answer those questions which might one day incriminate him. In that case, you are allowed to say that you don't want to answer a question. In this exceptional case, the Chamber may compel you to answer such a question, but they will tell you that there will be no consequences for you. And by doing that, the Chamber will award you a sort of immunity. I wanted to tell you this because this is -- this constitutes the rights of the accused [as interpreted] during any proceedings. I would also like to tell you that we are in the so-called oral proceedings. We don't have any written documents before us. We don't know anything about what you are going to say in answering your questions. So try and be as clear and precise as possible in your answers provided to both parties, because what you are going to say will appear on the screen in front of you in English. This will be the translation of your words. You can always refer to the screen if you read English. If not, you have to trust the interpreters who interpret either your words or the words of the parties in the -- to the proceedings. If at any point in time there are difficulties, you can always ask the party who has put the question to you to rephrase it and the Chamber will take care that the proceedings go on smoothly. The Defence counsel will have another information to give you concerning interpretation. I give the floor to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jusufspahic.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to save time I would kindly ask the usher to provide the Trial Chamber and our learned friends in the courtroom with a set of documents that I'm going to be using during the examination of this witness. This is to save us interrupting the course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, as the Presiding Judge has already told you, Mr. Jusufspahic, I have another information to give you. I would kindly ask you to make a pause before giving the answer to my question; this will allow the interpreters to interpret my question. This is my obligation when you provide your answer. If we don't do that, the Trial Chamber and our learned friends will not be able to follow what we are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. While this is being done I rise only with hesitation to perhaps suggest that we, prior to the commencement of the start of this witness's testimony, take a break. There's a relatively important matter that I feel I might need to discuss with my learned colleagues prior to their proceeding, which I think might actually be beneficial to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. If there are no objections on the part of the Defence, we are going to make a break and we shall resume around 20 or 15 minutes to 6.00, and we'll go until 7.00. The parties are going to discuss a certain matter during the break, and we shall resume at around quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. Did you sort out all the problems? No problems then. Okay. Mr. Usher, can you please accompany the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, can you tell us what your education is.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I have completed the post-secondary two-year school for pedagogy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war did you serve in the army and did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I did my regular military service in the former JNA and I was captain first class after I finished this service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by the President, you said that in 1992 you were in the municipal staff of the Zenica Territorial Defence. Can you please tell us in 1992 who were the commanders of the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: In 1992 the first commander was Jozo Jerkic. After him there was Branko Boncina who, before the war, had been the commander of that staff for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in the municipal staff of Zenica? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of operations and training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, did there come a time when there were organisational changes in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and did you change your employment or your post?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In November, I don't remember the precise date but it was in mid-November, two officers arrived from Sarajevo intending to establish some sort of command. At the time, we didn't know what sort of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in some way with the arrival of these two officers from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mustafa Poparic and I because we were from Zenica and we were familiar to a certain extent in the situation in Zenica were asked whether there was a building in Zenica where a command could be housed. And there were certain requirements that had to be met. We suggested engineering Zeljica [phoen], that building, because it met those requirements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn at that time who these officers were?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. At that time I didn't know either of them. Later on I found out who they were, but at that time I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you assisted in the search for a facility to house the new command, did you receive any orders on taking up new duties, on the transfer to new duties?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received an order that I was to go to the corps command, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond and that was the first time I learned that a corps command was being established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you then learned who these officers were and what their duties in the corps would be. Would you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These were two officers from Sarajevo, Enver Hadzihasanovic and Muradif Mekic. One was the commander and the other one was the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what were your duties in the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: The same as in the municipal staff. I was the operations organ in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was the beginning of the creation of the 3rd Corps, can you tell Their Honours what were the commander's priorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, we all had briefings together as there were not many of us. And the priorities were to set up the operations centre as soon as possible and to establish links or connections with the units as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the commander want to know the situation on the ground? Did you have a role in presenting or indicating the situation in the area where the 3rd Corps was to be?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. The war was going on, and one had to tour the territory. Some of the officers, together with the commander, toured the territory where the corps was to be set up, and I was part of that team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation you found on the territory you toured?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, there was chaos in every municipality, just like in Zenica. There were many fragmented units, many different commands, many commanders. Some units were acquiring a character of their own. This was all very fragmented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were the operations and training organ, do you know whether there was a re-organisation in the units in the area?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Of course there was re-organisation in the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to your duties in the operations and training organ, was there a requirement that an operations and training organ be designated and established so that it could carry out the functions that that organ had to do? What was done in this respect?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: When the commander ordered that the operations centre be established as soon as possible, quite truthfully I didn't really know what that meant. I was a reserve officer; I was not a professional officer. And I wasn't quite sure what an operations centre was, and he insisted that the operations centre be established as soon as possible. There were three of us operations men. Nehru Ganic was to be our chief but he was late in arriving. So we started, the three of us, and we didn't know anything about this. Ganic knew something more about this, but we started working.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, how did the operations and training organ function? What did it do? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: As you heard a little while ago, first of all we had to establish communications. No command can function if there are no communications. We established communications by means of radio stations which were not the kind that a corps was supposed to have. The real package communications were not set up until June so that in the operations centre we were handicapped by that fact. Then we didn't have the equipment we needed or the other things such as maps. I remember I brought the maps from the district staff, the TO staff I mean, whatever I was able to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you work? What were your tasks in fact?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Our first tasks were to receive reports from the units to see what the situation in the units was, to assist as far as we were able in carrying out their combat tasks. And the first order that was supposed to unify all this was written down at that time. And this was about the use of the units on the ground. We were the ones who were supposed to implement all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you received the reports from the units, were there other duties you had to do as the operations and training centre or organ?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every report from the terrain that we received, we collated these and we took note of what was important. Something has been switched off. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably pushed something inadvertently. It's all right now. When we received the reports, we wrote up our own report to the staffs of the superior command -- supreme command. We extracted information we considered important. And once in 24 hours we had to send a report of the command of the 3rd Corps to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that the three of you in the operations organ had no previous knowledge about the work of the operations and training centre. What was the staffing situation in the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: It was even worse in the subordinate units and we were able to see that from these reports. They were not proper combat reports. We could see how well-trained somebody was from the way they compiled a report, and the reports were received were terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the operations and training centre, were there certain office hours or was the work organised differently?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: We worked in shifts. There were three of us, and we changed shifts every 8 or 12 hours. And the same thing happened in the communications centre. We weren't there for 24 hours at a time. This was in a basement. You couldn't stand it for more than ten hours at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had to send reports to the superior command, that is the staff of the supreme command. Tell me, these reports, did they have to be sent by certain deadlines or did this depend on your own will when you were to send such reports?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: There were deadlines. And these deadlines forced us to send reports on time. This was usually by 2200 hours, as far as I can remember. The units of course had to submit their reports earlier. Very often they were late, so we had to rush when compiling our own report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, all the reports that arrived in the operations and training centre, did they reach the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't reach the corps commander. We in the operations organ would assess whether there was anything important. And if there was, we would report to him about it. But as for the regular reports, the daily reports that we compiled, we did that ourselves and sent them on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you did not deliver all the daily reports to the commander and, as you said, this was not possible, tell me who signed these reports.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: All the reports arriving from the subordinate units contained so much information, there were so many of these reports that had me submitted them all to the commander he would have been able to do nothing else but read those reports. That would have been impossible. We had to write a concise summary of what was in those reports, and then we would sign that at first. Later on that was changed and a duty operations officer was appointed and then he signed the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, tell me please, you said that first you established a packet communication with the supreme command regardless of the fact of who signed the document at first. Whose name and title were at the bottom of the documents sent by the package communication?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Usually -- no not usually, always the name was Enver Hadzihasanovic, and very often it said "SR," meaning he signed it in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the superior command or the organ to which something was send by a package communication and they received the document on which the name Enver Hadzihasanovic had been typed, did this mean that Enver Hadzihasanovic had actually signed the document?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't because they would get his name but not his Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond signature by this kind of communication. We would know who had signed it but they wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of everything you have just said, in this bundle of documents I have just shown you, would you please open to the second part which says "Operations and Training Organ," and would you please look at document P403. In response to my question you said that one of the first documents was a document where certain tasks were assigned to the subordinate units. Tell me, please, if you look at this document is this one of the documents assigning the tasks you have just mentioned, or is this document referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: This is one of the first documents issued by the corps command, and it designates the zones of responsibility of the various units. It's one of the first documents that the corps sent to its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, what was the role of the operations and training organ in preparing this and similar documents referring to combat activities or areas of combat responsibility of certain units? Did you play any role in all this?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to prepare all the elements the commander needed in order to issue such an order. We had to collect the information about the units. We even had to suggest to him how this order could be written.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this role of yours, tell me please, at any time was the entire territory ever established as the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, or did you ever prepare a document whereby the corps took over power -- took control over the entire territory?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that there is no such document referring to the corps, that the corps was responsible for the entire territory. But as for this document here, it refers to the zones or areas of defence connected to the line of defence. We didn't tell the commander that he was the main man in that zone. Everything was subordinated to the line of defence. So his area was designated with the two points to his left and right, referring to defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time were civilian authorities functioning in the same area as the area of defence of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was so-called War Presidencies, there was the Ministry of the Interior, whatever they were called; the civilian police. They had all the roles of government. The War Presidency took on the role of the government executive or assembly or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, you said you were not properly trained and the organs in the subordinate units were even more poorly trained. What was the policy of the command of the 3rd Corps in view of the training of you and superior commands? And if you took any measures, what measures did you take to improve the training?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: The position of the commander was that training was a priority. He repeated that from day one, from the first briefing. He told us that we should work as we went, that officers should be trained in order to be able to respond to tasks at hand. And we took all the possible measures to train operations officers in lower-ranking units, because we saw that people could not cope and that's what we did as we went along. Very often we would invite some people from the lower-ranking units to the corps to be trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 2, the following document. Mr. Jusufspahic, are you familiar with this document? Does this document reflect the way people were trained in order to make up an army in the given conditions?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I am very familiar with this document. The tasks that are listed here are to take stock of the troops, of the weapons, this we did all the time. We took stock of our units and we took measures accordingly. And this is our attempt to analyse the situation in the units in order to see what had to be done in order to improve things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that some of the reports were signed either by you or later on by operative officer on duty. Can you please look at document number 4. The date is 18 June 1993. Do you recognise this document? Do you know the person who drafted it and who signed it? The document is number 4.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I am familiar with the document. This is a regular command report to the staff of the command. This was drafted in June 1993, and a duty operations officer was I. Obviously I can't remember every single sentence, but this is how I did it. This is my handwriting. I remember that this is how our combat reports were written, and it was not just I who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document that was sent in mid-1993, does it reflect any changes or improvements in the way reports were drafted with regard to what you saw at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: At the beginning things were erratic. We did not know ourselves how things should be done. Later on an institution [as interpreted] was established and it was called a duty operations officer, and it was said that every duty operations officer should sign their report. And here you can see my name because I was the duty operations officer on the day. The officers affiliated with the command were duty operations officers, and they were the ones who signed those reports. And this is certainly an improvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, regardless of the efforts you made, did you still notice that there were more or less problems in the subordinate units? Could that have an influence on the establishment of the chain of command on the part of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: There were still problems, despite the training that we carried out. The training did not involve everybody, so there were still problems in reporting. For example, some reports did not arrive on time, or when they did they described the events that took place a long time ago. And then some people reported on particular fire being opened which was not important for the corps. Or they would report on things that were important but we had already learned about that thing through other channels. It happened very often that people reported erroneously, even the lines of defence they were manning. They would be off by several kilometres. Things would change from one day to another, and they failed to record that properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you observed those problems, did you react? Did you send any notification of that to the subordinate units? I believe that we issued an order or some sort of enactment in which we warned them how reports should be written, because the wrong reporting could have terrible consequences because we didn't know the real situation. I believe that we either issued an order or we retrained some of the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record the document was P160.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you look at the documents number 5 and 6. First can you look at document number 5. This is P271. Tell me, are you familiar with this document? Does it reflect exactly what you have just described for us, namely your efforts to observe and rectify problems that you faced with regard to your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I think that I might have been involved in its drafting. Us operative officers had a biggest bone to pick with those people who drafted bad reports, and this is a letter that we sent to all the subordinate units explaining in great detail what was wrong with the reports. But despite that, things did not improve that much even after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 6. This is P867. Can you please focus on items 2 and 3. And can you tell us why was the appropriate reporting important for the establishment of the normal chain of command at the level of a command such as a corps command? Are you familiar with this document? Do these items reflect the things that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: This is just one in a series of documents. There were more of such documents speaking about the importance of training. Other officers and other organs struggle to train their subordinate troops. This is just one of the documents requesting better training, which would ultimately Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond serve the interests of the entire command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, you have often signed those documents that were addressed to the staff of this frame [as interpreted] command and the commander did not see every of those reports. Who was it who decided which facts would be presented to the commander among those that had arrived from any of the superior -- subordinate commands?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was us, those who worked in the service and received those reports. That was at the beginning, the operative officers did that. The commander of the organ, if he was there, or somebody else. Later on it was the duty operations officer who did that. He would take a report from operative groups and if he had the time to do that, he could dwell upon those reports a bit longer. And sometimes he would just copy the sentences that he found in the reports of the operative group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, who was it who decided what relevant facts would be submitted in the reports to the supreme command staff? Which of the facts from the subordinate command reports were sent to the supreme command staff and who decided on that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: It was often the deputy commander or sometimes the commander himself, the chief of staff, their assistants. Whatever was sent regularly, it was us, duty operations officers, who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different topic. You have told us that you started working and learning on the job. In January, there were some combat activities. Did you in the operations centre have any information relative to the combat operations that took place in January? If that was the case, can you please share that information with us.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: In January, one of the first combat operations that the corps was involved in was when we received alarming reports from the sector of Vakuf and Novi Travnik about the fighting that was going on there. We received such reports. We looked at the overall situation and we tried to see how we could help those units there. This was our main preoccupation in the month of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time in January when you started receiving information from the areas that were closer to Zenica, closer than the ones where the combat operations were already underway in Gornji Travnik and Vakuf? Did you start receiving some information about the HVO forces coming closer to an area closer to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received a report from the Busovaca sector, from Kacin, about fighting going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you receive reports at that time? How did they reach you in the operations centre? By what ways and by what means did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: From the brigade we received reports through the regular communications means which were rather poor. First we would receive regular reports on the activities and movements of the HVO troops; later on we received different reports from different sides. The initial reports were those ones that we received from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent did you in the operations centre pay attention to these reports? Was there any link between those reports and the strategically important facilities or features in that area?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: As soon as we received the reports from Busovaca on the movements of the troops, not from the town of Busovaca but from the sector where our brigade was deployed, and as soon as there was fighting in that area, as soon as there was movement of forces, we immediately started thinking about a very important facility which was the Lasva junction. We tried to protect that facility even when I was a member of the TO of Zenica. It was a very important feature. It was the gateway to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the importance of that facility, did you in the operations and training centre, which was the body that pointed to the commander what the combat situation was, did you suggest to the commander or did you -- do you know whether the commander did anything, did he take any measures in order to prevent the Lasva junction from falling into any jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I did not write those orders, but I know that an order was issued to secure all the roads in the area including the junction. The only road towards the free territory went via Lasva and on, and there were orders issued in order to secure those roads, to keep them passable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know personally whether any sort of order was issued ordering that units should be used in combat? Was an order issued to attack villages in the vicinity of the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, such orders were not issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Jusufspahic, did there come a time when you start receiving -- when you started receiving information or reports in the operations centre about combat taking place in Lasva or in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: The first reports that we received from our units in the sector of Kacun and Busovaca spoke about movements. However, after that, after those regular reports, so to speak - they were not regular reports, they were interim reports, I suppose - we started receiving some other reports, not only from the command of one brigade, all of a sudden people started coming to the command with some verbal news about what was going on in the area. This is not customary, but this was what was going on. One piece of information followed another, and all that was rather alarming. Very often this was controversial and we didn't have the real insight into the situation; we didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you received information about some people being killed in that area?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put it this way: When the information is not timely and when you hear rumours, the first thing I heard, the first thing I remember is the killing of a commander. His name was Camdzic. He was my neighbour and I learned he had been killed. Again, I learned that from some sources that are not official, regular sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you were working as an officer in the army and there was combat, was it usual for different reports to arrive in the course of combat and only when the combat was over was the situation summed up, or did you have to have precise information at every moment as to what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: We had to have precise information for our commander, however it was very difficult to obtain it. We had to try and check to see what the real truth was. But as I told you, a lower-level commander would arrive, for example, with some news and we had to check it, we had to find ways and means of learning what was going on; that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the end, at the end of a day or on the following day did you deliver all the reports to the commander? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I remember that in the evening we were asked to write a summary of the situation and brief him. We would collect everything that we had checked, and I know that we delivered all the reports we received to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you can recall the reports you received in various ways, did any of the reports you received in the operations centre and passed on to the commander indicate that a crime might have been committed in the area, that there were grounds to suspect that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. These reports did not contain anything like that. We found nothing that might lead us to suspect such things had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a short while ago that news arrived about fighting in Busovaca. Tell me, do you know whether at a certain point in time there were certain agreements about the conflict in Busovaca and were you assigned any task in connection with these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We learned - everybody - knew this, that an agreement had been signed between the HVO and the army about a cease-fire and that a commission was being established to monitor this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were any meetings held in connection with this and were you involved in any way with the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, a meeting was held in Kakanj, I think in the hall of the Termoelektrana company. There were representatives of the HVO. As far as I recall there was Blaskic, we were there, our commander, and so was I. At that meeting operative details were agreed upon concerning the implementation of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally receive a task from the commander?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I had already received an order that I was to be one of the members of that commission; the others were Serif Kadric and the chief of the commission was Merdan, the deputy commander. At that meeting, and I remember it well, the commander initiated the following, that this commission that was to go out on to the ground to implement the fire was to carry certain orders with them, and he asked me to write these down on the spot. And I was taken aback and wondered how I was to do that. And he said, Take that to the representatives of the HVO and as soon as they agree to it, I'll sign it. So we drew up the order on the spot about the removal of the checkpoints, the passage of convoys, the return of the population to their homes, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, I will ask you to look at part 3 referring to the joint commission and to look at all these documents from 1 to 8 and tell me whether you recognise these documents.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Let me find it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the third part, III, joint commissions. Would you please look at the documents numbered 1 to 8. Do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I drew them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I take it that these are orders initiated by Commander Hadzihasanovic and later on signed by Commander Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we agreed in Kakanj, in the Termoelektrana building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the attitude of Commander Hadzihasanovic toward the implementation of these orders? Was this a purely formal acceptance or did he demand that this be strictly respected and complied with?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: He asked that this be strictly complied with. When he initiated these orders he simply decided that a stop should be put to all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at number 9, please. That's P140.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document reflect in your view the attitude of Commander Hadzihasanovic as to these orders were to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Working in the commission, we were duty-bound to draw up reports about what was going on and about the problems that we encountered. This is a warning to all the commands of the brigades, and they were instructed to make it possible for us to do whatever we had to on the ground. This shows that he had decided firmly that the conflict should be ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, what was the main task -- well, the main task is stated here, but how did you actually implement it?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, in the beginning it was very difficult, very, very difficult. There was a lot of mistrust among the local commanders on the ground, especially among the troops, and we spent a lot of time trying to convince various people that the other side would do the same. This is something they found hard to believe. So it was a very difficult job, especially to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the implementation of these orders on the cease-fire, did the commission deal with any other issues and who served these issues on you, so to speak, if you dealt with them?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Let me explain how we worked. We worked in teams. There were three representatives of the army and three representatives of the HVO in these commissions. In the morning on arrival at that house, the Hotel Tisa in Busovaca near the petrol pump, that's where we were, the chief of the European monitors, I think it was Thorpin [phoen], he would read the protest about the cease-fire. Then we would establish teams and go out on the ground to calm down the situation, but that was not our only task. In the commission we also received other requests from ordinary people. Because when people heard that there was some sort of commission there with the HVO, we started receiving requests that had nothing to do with combat activities. For example, that tank that had been captured by the HVO should be sent back. There were even requests from embassies, individuals, humanitarian organisations, all kinds of requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any requests by embassies?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the Iranian embassy as far as I can recall. There were others as well, but this one I remember because these people had been taken prisoner, at least that's what it said in the protest by HVO forces, and they had been brought to Kaonik prison in Busovaca. The Iranian embassy asked that we should check this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document numbered 12.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the protest.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the documents that the commission received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this request by the Iranian embassy or by humanitarian organisations or the one that arrived through the 3rd Corps and the mentioned foreigners, will you please tell us what sort of foreigners were these? Who were these foreigners that they were searching for?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Our information was that these were humanitarian workers who had arrived with aid or with money. That was all the information we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these protests and requests, how did the representatives of the HVO respond to these? Did they admit that they had arrested these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. They would not even admit that they had captured the two people who are in Kaonik. They refused to admit that these people were prisoners at all. I know two European monitors went to that prison to check this. They denied that this happened at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were working in this commission did you ever hear about Mujahedin or did you only discuss these persons as foreign humanitarian workers, as you describe them?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: They were not Mujahedin. I did not hear that expression at the time. These were humanitarian workers. Some people even said, we're not doing anything to get this aid to reach us, they're carrying money, driving good cars, and we were not doing anything to get these people to help us. That's what people said. I didn't hear the word "Mujahedin" being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time you personally encountered the expression "Mujahedin," and what duty were you performing at the time?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: The first time I came across that word, that expression, which I didn't even know what it meant, was as a member of the commission in Vitez, because the commission moved from Busovaca to Vitez. And that's when I heard this expression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours on what occasion you heard this expression and from whom.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: As the commission moved from Busovaca where the situation was under some sort of control to Vitez, where things were developing in a different direction and that was the reason for the move, the events in Ahmici took place, you know, the massacre in Ahmici. We didn't do that in the commission for a time, but then the European monitors insisted and I think that one of the first meetings after the work of the commission was re-established, I heard this word from Nakic, the word Mujahedin. We heard about an event that had happened in the village of Miletici, and that morning Nakic arrived very upset. And he said, While we are sitting here working, such things are happening up there. And I know they went to that village at once, Miletici, and upon their return he himself said that this had been done by Mujahedin who had entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that meeting of the commission or later on, did anyone in any way connect the event in Miletici to members of the BH army or was what Nakic said all that you learned about this event there?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: No, at least not as far as I could tell. I was there and neither the European monitors nor the HVO connected this to soldiers of the BH army. They didn't tell us, These are members of your army there, then, at the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me please, in connection with Ahmici, as a member of the commission did you have any personal knowledge about what had happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: When we moved to Vitez from Busovaca, we continued our regular work. I don't know how long this went on, but we went up there every day on a regular basis and went home in the evening. One morning we didn't go to that meeting. I saw in the corps that there was a kind of state of emergency, that there was something going on, that we wouldn't be going that day, and that's when I learned about the massacre in the corps. We didn't go that morning. After the European monitors insisted that we continue our work to prevent further escalation of the conflict, about a week later, it might have been more or less, I'm not sure exactly how long it was, we were very angry in the corps. We went to Vitez, and when we arrived there, a team was set up to go to Ahmici and I was part of that team. I think that the member of the joint commission for the HVO was a man called Tomo. I don't know his last name. And there was a European monitor and Bob Stewart, the commander of BritBat. We all went to the village in two vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you find there, briefly?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: It was terrible. It had all been burnt down; it was all gutted. I know that there was a house where the basement was still smoldering. A BritBat soldier found something that was small and charred. He was very upset and then I realised it was the corpse of a child. He couldn't stand it. He went out. And this made a deep impression on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufspahic, in the operations centre, what information or what data did you keep on your subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, please. In the operations centre we were supposed to have as many data on the subordinate units as possible, as many. Whatever we could collect we had to collect, and this all served for the commander's use on -- commander's decision on the use of these units. And we did what we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the operations centre, did you ever receive operation that in our units, the units of the 3rd Corps, there are also individuals who were foreigners or Mujahedin? While you were in the operations centre, up until mid-August, 1993, did you ever receive such information?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such information. The information that we had on the troops, armament, equipment, among all this information I did not come across information like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you inspected the ground, did you ever face the presence of foreigners in the area where the units of the 3rd Corps were active?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of my roles was to inspect some of the units, and that's where I encountered this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task? Which units did you visit, and what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of July or maybe mid-July, I remember that the strawberries were ripe when we were inspecting the ground. My task was to inspect a unit in the sector of the 312th Brigade, the so-called Karaula Battalion in the area of Bijelo Bucje. We were supposed to assist the commander at his own request because his battalion was on a very important axis. He wanted to organise defence in a forest; the commander didn't know how to do that. I went to inspect; I visited this unit. The chief of artillery was with me. He stayed with the artillery unit of the 312th Brigade, and I went uphill. And I worked out the problem with the commander. He helped him to organise defence in the forest. I told him where he should lay ambushes and where his points of defence should be. He was very happy. At the end of every visit, my last question is: Are there any other questions? Are there any more problems or any more requests for the corps command? I was already at the end of my visit, and just matter-of-factly he mentioned this, but not as a problem. He just mentioned a group of soldiers, some 30 of them. He said "Arabs." He said he didn't know who they were or what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that visit, did you visit any other units and did you face a similar problem there?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned from my visit to the 312th, I visited the command of one of the units of the 306th Mountain Brigade. I spoke to the chief of staff, the commander of the 1st Battalion, I believe that it was the 1st Battalion, and the operations officers from the OG Bosanska Krajina. I visited the area of Ljuta Greda. We paid a visit to the battalion, we inspected their line of fire. We issued orders how the line of defence should be amended and we returned to the battalion command. And again my question was: Are there any other requests? Are there any other questions? And then the commander whose name was Lubenovic, he was the commander of the 1st Battalion, told us that he had a problem with his fighters leaving for other units. His line of defence was very stretched and he was afraid that he could not be able to organise his shifts if the problem continued. He mentioned that there was some foreigners recruiting his fighters for themselves. And this was again when foreigners were mentioned in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: The commander always told us that whenever we visited units, that we should not bring him problems, that we should try and see what we could do ourselves. I asked to be taken to the spot, to the place where they were. I wanted to see whether there was anything I could do on the spot instead of bringing problems back to my commander. When I was taken to that place, there was a mosque in Mehurici and from the mosque you go through a little forest; this is where I was taken and I was shown the place where they were. And it is then that I saw a gate, something like a gate, and a fence that had existed maybe even before. There was an armed soldier standing at the gate. He was not wearing our uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC
utterances.text: We tried to enter. It -- this soldier was told that an officer from the corps command wanted to enter, but he would not allow us to come closer. He started taking his rifle off his shoulder, and I turned around with the other officers and we went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have some ten more questions for the witness tomorrow. I would like to show him two more documents, and I believe that my examination-in-chief will be finished very quickly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will continue tomorrow. Sir, you will have to come back tomorrow at 3.00. Please be at the disposal of the Tribunal to be present here around 3.00 for the beginning of tomorrow's session. As you have already been told by the Defence, your testimony will be finished very quickly tomorrow. From now on, you're not supposed to speak to any of the parties because you have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you are no longer in the position to talk to the Defence. We will adjourn and we will resume tomorrow at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of January, 2005, at 3.00 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
